\chapter{The First Verbs}
\label{ch:first-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{5}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can build short present-tense Tamil sentences with the chapter's first verbs.}

Build a short present-tense sentence about yourself out loud — speak, live, work — by putting the stem, the present marker and the person ending together.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[pēsu]{\ta{பேசு} (pēsu) — \textquotedblleft{}to speak,\textquotedblright{} your first full verb}

\label{lesson:TA-C05-pesu}



\begin{quote}
So far, \textquotedblleft{}to be.\textquotedblright{} Here is a verb that \emph{does} something — and it shows how Tamil builds \textquotedblleft{}I do X.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ta{பேசு}} (\emph{pēsu}, \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{}) is native Dravidian. The bare stem \emph{pēsu} is also the command \textquotedblleft{}speak!\textquotedblright{} To say \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I speak},\textquotedblright{} Tamil adds a two-part ending to the stem: \textbf{tense} + \textbf{person}:

\begin{quote}
\emph{pēsu-} (speak) + \emph{-giṟ-} (present) + \emph{-ēṉ} (\textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ \emph{\textbf{pēsugiṟēṉ}}, \textquotedblleft{}I speak.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The \emph{\textbf{-ēṉ}} ending \emph{is} \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} — so, as with \emph{irukkiṟēṉ}, you rarely need the word \emph{nāṉ}. Change the ending, change the person: \emph{pēsugiṟāṉ} (\textquotedblleft{}he speaks\textquotedblright{}), \emph{pēsugiṟāḷ} (\textquotedblleft{}she speaks\textquotedblright{}), \emph{pēsugiṟārgaḷ} (\textquotedblleft{}they/you-respectful speak\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: stem + tense + person}]
Every Tamil verb is built this way — a stem, a tense-marker, a person-ending, stacked in that order and glued together. Learn the pattern once and every verb follows it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pēsu\textquotedblright{} (speak!)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{} — \emph{pēsugiṟēṉ}
  \item the three stacked pieces (stem \emph{pēsu} + present \emph{-giṟ-} + \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} \emph{-ēṉ})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Build \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{} from \emph{pēsu}, and name the three pieces of a Tamil verb. (\emph{Pēsugiṟēṉ}; stem + tense + person.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nāṉ tamiḻ pēsugiṟēṉ]{\ta{நான்} \ta{தமிழ்} \ta{பேசுகிறேன்} (nāṉ tamiḻ pēsugiṟēṉ) — \textquotedblleft{}I speak Tamil\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TA-C05-naan-tamizh-pesugiren}



\begin{quote}
Your first full, moving sentence — and it names the language itself, with a sound almost no other language has.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ta{நான்} \ta{தமிழ்} \ta{பேசுகிறேன்}} = \textbf{\ta{நான்}} (\emph{nāṉ}, \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\ta{தமிழ்}} (\emph{tamiḻ}, \textquotedblleft{}Tamil,\textquotedblright{} the object) + \textbf{\ta{பேசுகிறேன்}} (\emph{pēsugiṟēṉ}, \textquotedblleft{}speak\textquotedblright{}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I Tamil speak},\textquotedblright{} the verb last as always. The name \textbf{\ta{தமிழ்}} (\emph{tamiḻ}) is native, of debated but clearly Dravidian origin (often linked to a sense of \textquotedblleft{}sweetness / one's own speech\textquotedblright{}); it names one of the oldest living literary languages in the world, with poetry two thousand years old still read today.

That final sound is worth dwelling on. The \emph{ḻ} of \emph{tamiḻ} is a curled retroflex sitting somewhere between an \emph{r}, an \emph{l} and a \emph{zh} — rare enough among the world's languages that Tamil is sometimes called \textquotedblleft{}the \emph{ḻ} language.\textquotedblright{} Getting it approximately right matters more than getting it perfect; nobody will mistake what you mean.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: no gender on \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{}}]
Notice \emph{pēsugiṟēṉ} is the same whether a man or a woman says it — Tamil marks \textbf{no gender in the first or second person} (only the third: \emph{pēsugiṟāṉ} he / \emph{pēsugiṟāḷ} she). This is unlike Hindi, where even \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{} changes for a male or female speaker (\emph{boltā/boltī}). Tamil saves gender for \textquotedblleft{}he/she/it.\textquotedblright{}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nāṉ tamiḻ pēsugiṟēṉ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the special Tamil sound in \emph{tamiḻ} (the retroflex \emph{ḻ})
  \item does \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{} change for a man vs. a woman? (No — Tamil marks no gender in the 1st person)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I speak Tamil,\textquotedblright{} and name the rare sound in the word \emph{tamiḻ}. (\emph{Nāṉ tamiḻ pēsugiṟēṉ}; the retroflex \emph{ḻ} — \ta{ழ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[va, ka]{\ta{வ} and \ta{க} — the vowel inside each consonant}

\label{lesson:TA-W01-abugida-va-ka}



\begin{quote}
Tamil's letters do not join and they carry many curves. Now learn the sound that arrives for free inside every consonant.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: The vowel you get for free}
Tamil is an \textbf{abugida}, like Devanagari: a consonant already contains a vowel.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{க} is not \textquotedblleft{}k\textquotedblright{}. \ta{க} is \textquotedblleft{}ka\textquotedblright{}.}
\end{quote}

Every consonant carries a built-in \textbf{a} until a later mark removes or replaces it.

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{வ} — \textquotedblleft{}va\textquotedblright{}}
1. \textbf{a near-closed loop on the left} 2. \textbf{a full-height arm across the top, ending in a descender on the right}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{க} — \textquotedblleft{}ka\textquotedblright{}}
1. \textbf{a straight horizontal top bar} 2. \textbf{a bowl hanging from its left end} 3. \textbf{a short right stroke that hooks left below}

\begin{sounds}
Devanagari separates \dv{क}, \dv{ख}, \dv{ग}, \dv{घ}. Tamil uses \textbf{\ta{க}} across that space: \emph{k} at the start of a word and when doubled (\textbf{\ta{க்க}}), \emph{g} after a nasal (\textbf{\ta{ங்க}}), and a softer \emph{h}-like sound between vowels. \textbf{Position}, not a new spelling, selects the sound.

Tamil therefore needs only 18 consonant letters where Devanagari needs 33; its native words do not depend on those written distinctions.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens}]
\textbf{One letter, three sounds — now on the page.} Chapter\textasciitilde{}1 said Tamil picks this sound by position rather than by spelling; here is the letter that does it. Devanagari spells \emph{ka}, \emph{kha}, \emph{ga} and \emph{gha} with four separate letters. Tamil writes \ta{க} for all of them: \emph{k} at the start of a word and when doubled (\ta{க்க}), \emph{g} after a nasal (\ta{ங்க}), and a softer \emph{h}-like sound between vowels. That is why Tamil needs only 18 consonant letters where Devanagari needs 33 — its native words do not depend on those written distinctions.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ta{வ} — \textquotedblleft{}left loop, top arm, descender\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ta{க} — \textquotedblleft{}top bar, left bowl, hooking right stroke\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}\ta{க} is \textbf{ka}, not k\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} initial \emph{k} · after a nasal \emph{g} · between vowels soft \emph{h}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ta{க}} say alone? (\textbf{Ka} — the vowel is inherent.) What kind of script is this? (An \textbf{abugida}.) Which sounds can \ta{க} spell? (\emph{k}, \emph{g}, and a softer \emph{h}-like sound, chosen by \textbf{position}.) Draw \textbf{\ta{வ}} and \textbf{\ta{க}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vāḻ]{\ta{வாழ்} (vāḻ) — \textquotedblleft{}to live, to flourish\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TA-C05-vaazh}



\begin{quote}
A second verb — and one of the most beloved words in the language, the one Tamils use to bless.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ta{வாழ்}} (\emph{vāḻ}, \textquotedblleft{}to live, to flourish, to thrive\textquotedblright{}) is native Dravidian, and carries more warmth than a plain \textquotedblleft{}to reside.\textquotedblright{} From it grow \emph{vāḻkkai} (\textquotedblleft{}life\textquotedblright{}) and the blessing \emph{vāḻga} (\textquotedblleft{}may you live / long live\textquotedblright{}), heard in \emph{vāḻga tamiḻ} (\textquotedblleft{}long live Tamil\textquotedblright{}). To say \textquotedblleft{}I live,\textquotedblright{} add the familiar ending: \emph{\textbf{nāṉ … vāḻgiṟēṉ}}, stem + present \emph{-giṟ-} + \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} \emph{-ēṉ}, exactly like \emph{pēsugiṟēṉ}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: same engine, new verb}]
You already know the machine: \emph{vāḻ-} (stem) + \emph{-giṟ-} (present) + \emph{-ēṉ} (\textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ \emph{vāḻgiṟēṉ} (\textquotedblleft{}I live\textquotedblright{}). Every verb you learn slots into the same three-part frame — that is the reward for learning \emph{pēsu} carefully.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vāḻ\textquotedblright{} — feel the retroflex \emph{ḻ}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I live\textquotedblright{} — \emph{nāṉ vāḻgiṟēṉ}
  \item the blessing — \emph{vāḻga!} (\textquotedblleft{}long live / may you flourish\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Build \textquotedblleft{}I live\textquotedblright{} from \emph{vāḻ}, and give the blessing made from it. (\emph{Vāḻgiṟēṉ}; \emph{vāḻga!}, \textquotedblleft{}may you live / long live.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vēlai sey]{\ta{வேலை} \ta{செய்} (vēlai sey) — \textquotedblleft{}to work\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TA-C05-velai-sey}



\begin{quote}
The last verb of the chapter — and, like Hindi's \emph{karnā}, it is a \textquotedblleft{}do\textquotedblright{} verb that builds a hundred others.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ta{செய்}} (\emph{sey}, \textquotedblleft{}to do, to make\textquotedblright{}) is a core native Dravidian verb, and Tamil — like Hindi with \emph{karnā} — builds compound verbs by putting a noun in front of it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ta{வேலை} \ta{செய்}} (\emph{vēlai sey}) = \textquotedblleft{}work-do\textquotedblright{} = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to work}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{vēlai}, \textquotedblleft{}work\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\ta{சமையல்} \ta{செய்}} (\emph{samaiyal sey}) = \textquotedblleft{}to cook\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{\textbf{udavi sey}} = \textquotedblleft{}to help\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

So \textquotedblleft{}I work\textquotedblright{} is \emph{\textbf{nāṉ vēlai seygiṟēṉ}} — \emph{sey-} + \emph{-giṟ-} + \emph{-ēṉ}, \textquotedblleft{}I do work.\textquotedblright{} Master \emph{sey} and a whole grammar of \textquotedblleft{}do-verbs\textquotedblright{} opens up.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: noun + \ta{செய்} = a new verb}]
This \textquotedblleft{}noun + \emph{sey}\textquotedblright{} pattern is the exact twin of Hindi's \textquotedblleft{}noun + \emph{karnā}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{kām karnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to work\textquotedblright{}). Two unrelated language families — Dravidian and Indo-Aryan — landed on the same clever trick: make an all-purpose \textquotedblleft{}do\textquotedblright{} verb, then bolt nouns onto it. Living side by side for millennia, Tamil and Hindi have quietly traded habits like this.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vēlai sey\textquotedblright{} (to work)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I work\textquotedblright{} — \emph{nāṉ vēlai seygiṟēṉ}
  \item the Hindi twin of this trick (noun + \emph{karnā})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Tamil turn \textquotedblleft{}work\textquotedblright{} into \textquotedblleft{}to work,\textquotedblright{} and what Hindi verb works the same way? (\emph{Vēlai} + \emph{sey} = \textquotedblleft{}work-do\textquotedblright{}; Hindi's \emph{karnā}, as in \emph{kām karnā}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 5 — The first verbs}

\label{lesson:TA-C05-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Three verbs, one engine — build real sentences about yourself.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn — build the sentences}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I speak Tamil\textquotedblright{} — \emph{nāṉ tamiḻ pēsugiṟēṉ}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I live in Chennai\textquotedblright{} — \emph{nāṉ Cheṉṉaiyil vāḻgiṟēṉ}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I work\textquotedblright{} — \emph{nāṉ vēlai seygiṟēṉ}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}he speaks\textquotedblright{} vs. \textquotedblleft{}she speaks\textquotedblright{} — \emph{pēsugiṟāṉ} / \emph{pēsugiṟāḷ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — the engine}]
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three stacked pieces of every Tamil verb (stem + tense + person)
  \item the ending that means \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} (\emph{-ēṉ})
  \item where Tamil marks gender — and where it doesn't (3rd person only)
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — roots you now carry}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pēsu} \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{} (native Dravidian)
  \item \emph{vāḻ} \textquotedblleft{}to live/flourish\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \emph{vāḻkkai} \textquotedblleft{}life,\textquotedblright{} \emph{vāḻga} \textquotedblleft{}long live\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{sey} \textquotedblleft{}to do\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \emph{vēlai sey} \textquotedblleft{}to work\textquotedblright{} (the twin of Hindi's \emph{karnā})
  \item \emph{tamiḻ} — the language, and its signature retroflex \emph{ḻ}
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
In one breath, say your language and your work in Tamil, then bless someone with the \emph{vāḻ} verb. (\emph{Nāṉ tamiḻ pēsugiṟēṉ. Nāṉ vēlai seygiṟēṉ. Vāḻga!})
\end{tcolorbox}
